title: Apparition Trail tours visit Old Town's spookiest sites
excerpt: It's spooky season and the spirits are stirring in downtown Winchester.
content:
It's spooky season and the spirits are stirring in downtown Winchester.

If you'd like to hear some of the eeriest stories about Old Town's most mysterious denizens, you're in luck because The Apparition Trail passes through several well-known haunts and introduces you to the ghosts that have made Winchester their forever home.

Tour host April Allred said specters generally don't put on a grandiose display like they do in movies like "Ghostbusters," but instead prefer a low-key afterlife.

"A lot of times, we think of ghost stories as these big, giant things, but usually it's the many small things that point to a place being haunted," Allred said.

An example is the Shenandoah Valley Civil War Museum on the Loudoun Street Mall, which occupies the former Frederick County Courthouse that was built in 1840 and, during the Civil War, served as a prison, a hospital and barracks for both Union and Confederate soldiers.

Allred said a person who works at the Civil War Museum has reported instances that defy rational explanation.

"He says when he's walking around, sometimes he'll just run into an intensely cold spot and it kind of just passes through him, and in that moment, he's just overtaken by this deep sense of sadness and nostalgia for the past," Allred said. "But then as soon as it comes, it leaves and disappears as if he has collided with a ghost on a different plane, a different dimension."

No one knows for sure whose spirit could be causing the cold spots, but Allred suspects it's the echo of a Civil War prisoner who was held in the courthouse in the 1860s.

Behind the Shenandoah Valley Civil War Museum is another well-known building that is said to be haunted: Rouss City Hall at 15 N. Cameron St.

The building opened in 1901, almost four decades after the Civil War ended, but the land where it stands was a hotspot of activity during the war. Federal troops staged and camped there whenever the Union occupied the city — Winchester changed hands more than 70 times — and Black soldiers with the 19th United States Colored Troops bivouacked at the site. Additionally, the property saw action during the Second Battle of Winchester on June 13-15, 1863.

"People have seen soldiers outside, walking around or kind of holding onto bars and peering out while somebody stands behind them holding a gun," Allred said. "For a lot of the soldiers who stayed there, it was their last days before they passed away [in battle]."

Allred said the previous owner of The Apparition Trail tour, J.P. Murphy of Winchester, believes that Winchester's most famous daughter used to linger in the building that now accommodates Murphy Beverage Co. on the Loudoun Street Mall.

Patsy Cline was born in Winchester and spent most of her teenage years living with her mother and siblings in a house at 608 S. Kent St., less than a mile from Murphy Beverage. She had a brief but brilliant career as a country singer before dying at the age of 30 in a plane crash on March 5, 1963, in Tennessee.

According to Allred, a man was staying in an apartment above Murphy Beverage several years after Cline's death. He struggled to pay rent on time but, just as Murphy was ready to evict him, the man said he had landed a job as a docent at Cline's former residence, which had been converted into a museum called the Patsy Cline Historic House.

Murphy, knowing that docents are usually unpaid volunteers, didn't know how his tenant's new job would pay the bills, but he agreed to give the man a second chance.

"Somehow he started paying his rent month after month," Allred said. "But then one day, he just skipped town."

During the three months that the man had been working at the Patsy Cline Historic House, Murphy told Allred that other tenants above Murphy Beverage sometimes heard late-night knocking on their doors and walls but, when they checked, no one was there.

Murphy later discovered that his former tenant had been arrested for skimming money from the Patsy Cline Historic House. From the time of the man's arrest onward, Allred said, the knocking was heard no more.

Putting the pieces together, Allred said she suspects Cline, who had little patience with unscrupulous businessmen who pocketed money that she had earned from her performances, had been knocking on the apartment doors above Murphy Beverage because she wanted the man who was stealing from her family's house to pay them back.

"When it was done," Allred said, referring to the former tenant's arrest, "she said, 'OK, I'm going back to my regular haunts.'"

Skeptics would argue that there are no records of a man taking from the Patsy Cline Historic House, but they're missing the point: Ghost stories are fun as long as you're willing to suspend a bit of disbelief.

Allred's family-friendly Apparition Trail tour visits these Old Town haunts and more. If you want to check it out before Halloween, reserve a ticket now because spots are filling fast. In fact, Tuesday's tour is already sold out, but there are still openings for Monday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. All tours start at 8 p.m. at Handley Library and take about 90 minutes, so Allred advises you to wear comfortable shoes and "go to the bathroom beforehand because there's nowhere on the tour to do that."

Tickets for the Apparition Trail cost $20 each for adults, while children 12 and under can tag along for free. Reserve your spot now at apparitiontrail.com.

If you're not up for walking through downtown Winchester, Allred has some other ghost stories from throughout the Northern Shenandoah Valley that she'll be telling today at 6 p.m. at Fable Greenhouse and Gardens (formerly Horton's Nursery) at 2731 Front Royal Pike near Winchester. The event is free and all attendees will receive 10% off any greenhouse purchases. For more information, visit https://bit.ly/4sgAus0.

And one more thing. Allred is collecting ghost stories from across the region and plans on sharing them in a future book. If you have a tale to tell, call her at 540-692-6366.
